Background: Leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by infection with Mycobacterium leprae. Drug resistance can occur when M. leprae undergoes changes that allow it to survive and multiply even in the presence of the standard drug. The aim of this study was to evaluate primary resistance of M. leprae to single and multiple drugs by testing skin biopsy homogenates obtained from patients with lepromatous leprosy.
Methods: Skin biopsies from three patients with lepromatous leprosy without prior history of antileprosy treatment were used in this study. Skin biopsy homogenates were injected into the footpads of 90 BALB/c mice. After injection, the mice were treated with single or multiple drugs, and their responses were observed. The results of the drug treatments were also compared with the results of culture and growth of M. leprae under laboratory conditions.
Results: The M. leprae isolated from the skin biopsy homogenates were found to be sensitive to all single drugs (rifampicin, clofazimine, dapsone) and combinations of these three drugs. However, after 268 days, rifampicin and dapsone were found to lose their activity, and only clofazimine was able to inhibit the growth of M. leprae.
Conclusion: In this mouse footpad model, M. leprae from the skin biopsy homogenates of patients with lepromatous leprosy showed primary resistance to a combination of rifampicin and dapsone, but not to clofazimine.

**Abstract**

Serotonin or melatonin was infused into the third cerebral ventricle (3rd V) or into the medial basal hypothalamus (MBH) of both intact ewes and ewes with lesions of the anterior hypothalamic area. To evaluate the effect of these indoleamines and their site of action on the hypothalamic centers involved in the control of luteinizing hormone (LH) release and ovulation in sheep, experiments were conducted. Infusion of serotonin into either the 3rd V or MBH of intact ewes increased the number of LH releasing hormone (LHRH) neurones in the MBH, which resulted in an increase in plasma LH. In contrast, infusing serotonin into the MBH of ewes with lesions of the anterior hypothalamic area only increased the number of LHRH neurones, but did not increase plasma LH concentrations. The data obtained suggest that serotonin is an indirect stimulant of LH release and has its site of action in the MBH. When serotonin enters the MBH it stimulates LHRH neurones, which increases the amount of LHRH in the hypophysiotropic (hypothalamo-pituitary) tract, thereby stimulating the pituitary to increase the amount of LH in the blood.

The effect of melatonin was the opposite to that of serotonin: when melatonin was infused into the 3rd V of either intact ewes or ewes with lesions of the anterior hypothalamic area, it had no effect on the number of LH-releasing hormone (LHRH) neurons, but inhibited the increase in the amount of LH in the blood. This suggests that melatonin has a direct inhibitory effect on the pituitary.

This work contributes to understanding the role of serotonin and melatonin on ovulation control and can have implications on the study of ovulation control in other animals as well as potentially be used for inducing ovulation in ewes.

Serotonin or melatonin was infused into the third cerebral ventricle (3rd V) or into the medial basal hypothalamus (MBH) of both intact ewes and ewes with lesions of the anterior hypothalamic area. To evaluate the effect of these indoleamines and their site of action on the hypothalamic centers involved in the control of luteinizing hormone (LH) release and ovulation in sheep, experiments were conducted. Infusion of serotonin into either the 3rd V or MBH of intact ewes increased the number of LH releasing hormone (LHRH) neurones in the MBH, which resulted in an increase in plasma LH. In contrast, infusing serotonin into the MBH of ewes with lesions of the anterior hypothalamic area only increased the number of LHRH neurones, but did not increase plasma LH concentrations. The data obtained suggest that serotonin is an indirect stimulant of LH release and has its site of action in the MBH. When serotonin enters the MBH it stimulates LHRH neurones, which increases the amount of LHRH in the hypophysiotropic (hypothalamo-pituitary) tract, thereby stimulating the pituitary to increase the amount of LH in the blood.

The effect of melatonin was the opposite to that of serotonin: when melatonin was infused into the 3rd V of either intact ewes or ewes with lesions of the anterior hypothalamic area, it had no effect on the number of LH-releasing hormone (LHRH) neurons, but inhibited the increase in the amount of LH in the blood. This suggests that melatonin has a direct inhibitory effect on the pituitary.

Abstract

The family is a social entity that is fundamental to the development of children into mature, functional adults. Currently, traditional family values that have been passed down through generations appear to be at risk. This has significant implications for the stability and health of individuals, families, and communities. This article explores selected issues related to intergenerational transmission of family values. These include:
1. The definition of family tradition and how it is passed down from one generation to another.
2. Reasons why some family values can be lost from a family.
3. How cultural and economic changes affect the transmission of family values and what this means for the future of the family.
4. How the loss of or change in family values affect children as they become mature and have their own families.

This research reviews existing literature on the topic and uses examples to illustrate points. This research aims to help explain the importance of family values and help individuals, families, and communities preserve those values, which are important to the stability and health of all three.

This paper proposes a hierarchical control architecture designed for an arbitrary high voltage multiterminal dc (MTDC) network. In the proposed architecture, the primary control of the MTDC system is decentralized and implemented using a generalized droop strategy. Designing the hierarchical structure was necessary to solve the problems that arise when a large number of converter stations are connected in a large MTDC network. The controller design method takes into account the power losses that arise from current injection into the grid at the stations where the power is being injected and power extraction from the grid where the power is being extracted.

The secondary control, which is centralized, uses optimal power flow (OPF) to minimize active power losses on the DC side of the MTDC network. The OPF solution is obtained iteratively. Simulation results were obtained to validate the control scheme, using the PSCAD/EMTDC simulation tool. A simple network, containing one AC station and two DC stations, as well as more complex network containing three AC stations and four DC stations, were used in the simulations. Both networks contain single-phase, four-pulse converters. This research shows that the proposed hierarchical control architecture has good stability and good tracking, and can be implemented in both small and large MTDC networks.

**Abstract**

Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) mediate distinct biological responses by activating similar intracellular signaling pathways. Whether the specificity of the response is due to qualitative or quantitative differences in the signaling output has not been established. We addressed this question by coupling Met receptor tyrosine kinase to the pathways mediated either by Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) or ErbB3. We found that coupling Met to EGFR downstream signaling pathways resulted in proliferation. Coupling Met to ErbB3 downstream signaling pathways resulted in survival. This indicates that the specificity of the cell response is due to the quality of the signaling output and not the quantity. The mechanism underlying these differences was further analyzed in detail. Our study shows that the coupling of Met to different signaling pathways causes different cellular developmental outcomes.
